name: Galle
tagline: A Dutch-era fortified town on a rocky headland, with ramparts, a lighthouse, boutique shops and cafés in a living UNESCO fort.
highlight: Walking the ramparts of Galle Fort at sunset, with waves crashing below and the lighthouse glowing.
shortDescription: A 17th-century Dutch fort that is still a living community, with ramparts, a lighthouse, mosques and churches, boutiques, cafés and the beaches of the south coast nearby.
metaDescription: A Galle travel guide: Galle Fort ramparts and lighthouse, the clock tower, Dutch Reformed Church, Meeran Mosque, boutiques and cafés, Unawatuna beach, where to stay and a two-day plan.

image.alt: The ramparts and white lighthouse of Galle Fort

intro: Galle is a city on the south-west coast, and its historic heart, the Galle Fort, is one of the best-preserved colonial sea fortresses in Asia. The Portuguese built the first fort in 1588, and the Dutch took the town in 1640 and constructed the massive stone ramparts and bastions visible today. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and unlike many such sites, it is a living town, with shops, schools, mosques, churches and families inside the walls.

The fort covers about 52 hectares, and a walk along the ramparts, about 2.5 km, takes in the lighthouse, the Old Gate, the Clock Tower and sea views. Inside, streets are lined with Dutch-colonial houses, some converted into boutique hotels, antique shops, galleries and cafés. Landmarks include the Dutch Reformed Church of 1755, the Meeran Mosque and the National Museum.

The 2004 tsunami hit Galle hard, but the fort's thick walls protected the old town. Beyond the walls, the south coast has beaches such as Unawatuna and Jungle Beach, and a stilt fishermen coastline at Koggala. Two days is a good stay, ideally with sunset on the ramparts.

whyVisit.intro: Galle is Sri Lanka's most charming colonial town.
